observations: ct-radio renders a native <input type="radio"> and a composed <ct-label> for its visible text — no images, icons, or other non-text content of its own.

standard: 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (Level A)

observations: Unlike ct-input, ct-radio does compose a real <ct-label> internally (mirroring upstream radio.twig's include of civictheme:label) rather than punting labelling to the implementer entirely. However, ct-label's own <label for="..."> renders inside ct-label's OWN separate shadow root, so the `for`/`id` reference still cannot resolve across that shadow boundary to reach ct-radio's <input> — id references are resolved within a single tree scope, and composing two custom elements as siblings does not create one tree for this purpose. ct-radio mitigates this by mirroring `label`/`ariaLabel` onto the input's own `aria-label` (see 4.1.2), so a working accessible name exists regardless of the broken visual/programmatic label link. A second, separate 1.3.1 concern: a *set* of related radios sharing one `name` is conventionally grouped under a `<fieldset>`/`<legend>` (via ct-label with `tag="legend"`) so assistive technology understands they form one question — ct-radio, like upstream radio.twig, is a single-control component and does not render that wrapping fieldset itself; that composition is the implementer's (or a future ct-radio-group molecule's) responsibility.

The `autocomplete` attribute this criterion concerns is not meaningful for a radio input in the way it is for text fields, and is not exposed as a property (matching CivicTheme's own radio.component.yml, which has no autocomplete field).

The `invalid` state is conveyed through a border/background color change (plus `aria-invalid="true"` for assistive technology) and the checked state is conveyed through both a color change and a filled-dot shape change (not color alone) — but ct-radio renders no icon or text of its own to describe *why* an invalid radio is invalid. Compliance depends on the implementer always pairing an invalid group with a visible text description (e.g. an adjacent ct-field-message), not relying on the red border alone.

The composed ct-label's text color (overridden via the `--ct-label-light/dark-color` custom property to use ct-radio's own body-toned color tokens rather than ct-label's default heading-toned one, so that the option text matches CivicTheme's actual radio-label color intent) meets the minimum 4.5:1 contrast ratio against the background in both themes, using the same token pairing relied on elsewhere in this design system.
The label text is rendered by ct-label using rem-based typography tokens and remains visible/readable when resized to at least 200%.
All label text is rendered as real text via the composed ct-label, never as an image.
The radio circle has a fixed small footprint by design (matching the native control), and the label text wraps normally with no fixed width or clipping.

The border color in the default, hover, checked, and invalid states meets 3:1 contrast against the surrounding background in both light and dark themes, using CivicTheme's existing border/interaction/error tokens.
Label text remains visible/readable when line spacing, letter spacing, and word spacing are increased per this criterion's thresholds, since nothing clips or truncates it.

standard: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA)
observations: ct-radio introduces no additional content on hover or focus beyond the native focus-visible outline and a border-width/color change.

A single ct-radio is fully keyboard-operable (Tab to focus, Space to check) via its native <input>. The gap is at the *group* level: native browser radio-button grouping — mutual exclusivity and arrow-key roving between same-`name` radios — is scoped by the HTML standard to controls sharing one DOM tree, and each ct-radio's <input> lives in its own separate shadow root. Arrow-key roving between grouped ct-radio instances is therefore NOT reproduced natively and is not implemented by this component (out of scope for a single-atom port; see the class doc comment). ct-radio does include a best-effort JS mitigation that enforces mutual exclusivity (unchecking other same-`name` radios on `change`), but a keyboard user relying on arrow keys to move between options in a group will not get the native behavior they'd expect from a plain HTML radio group.
The native <input> introduces no keyboard trap; focus moves in and out normally via Tab/Shift+Tab.

standard: 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A)

observations: ct-radio is a single focusable element that participates in the natural document tab order; it does not manipulate tabindex or focus order itself.
ct-radio renders no links.
Compliance depends on the implementer supplying `label` text that specifically and clearly names this option within its group (e.g. "Email", not "Option 1").
The component's own CSS always renders a solid focus-visible outline (`--ct-radio-{theme}-outline-color`, width/offset tokens) regardless of implementer configuration.
Nothing in ct-radio's own rendering overlaps or hides its focus indicator; obscuring it would require page-level layout outside this component's control.

Activation uses the native <input> click/change behavior; the composed ct-label's click handler only forwards a synthetic `.click()` to the input, which itself follows standard pointer-cancellation semantics.

The accessible name always comes from `aria-label`, which defaults to the visible `label` text verbatim — so the two can never diverge unless an implementer deliberately overrides `ariaLabel` with different text.

The radio circle itself is 1.625rem (26px) square, which clears the 24x24 CSS pixel minimum on its own. Clicking the composed ct-label's text also activates the input (via the manual click-forwarding mitigation for 1.3.1's broken for/id link), which meaningfully extends the effective target — but that extension is a best-effort JS behavior, not a native, guaranteed one, so compliance for the *combined* target still depends on the implementer not overriding or removing that behavior.
Compliance depends on the implementer setting the correct lang attribute on the html element; not something a single form control can affect.
Compliance depends on the implementer setting lang attributes on parts of the page that differ from the main language.
ct-radio introduces no side effects on focus beyond the native focus-visible style change — no auto-navigation, auto-submission, or other unexpected context change.

Selecting a radio only updates this component's own `checked` state and, per the group-exclusivity mitigation, unchecks other same-`name` ct-radio elements — no auto-submission or forced navigation is bundled into the component.
Compliance depends on the implementer using the same visual presentation and consistent option labeling for the same kind of choice everywhere it recurs across the site.

Setting `invalid` gives the radio a red border and `aria-invalid="true"`, which identifies *that* an error exists on that option, but ct-radio renders no text describing *what* the error is. Compliance depends on the implementer pairing an invalid group with a text description (e.g. ct-field-message) — and, per the 1.3.1 caveat, `aria-describedby` pointing from ct-radio's inner <input> to an id on a sibling custom element's host will not resolve across the shadow-DOM boundary either, so today there is no working *programmatic* link between the two; only their visual adjacency conveys the relationship.

ct-radio provides its own visible option label via the composed ct-label, but provides no group-level instructions (e.g. "Select one") of its own; compliance depends on the implementer supplying that context, typically via a ct-label with `tag="legend"` wrapping the whole group.
Compliance depends entirely on the implementer providing a correction suggestion in an accompanying text component (e.g. ct-field-message); ct-radio has no mechanism to render suggestion text itself.

Role (radio) and checked/disabled/required state come for free from the native <input type="radio">, always correctly exposed regardless of implementer input. The accessible name is always populated (`aria-label`, defaulting to `label` text — see 2.5.3), so a single ct-radio never lacks a name the way an unlabelled ct-input can. The genuine gap is group identity: assistive technology's "N of M" radio-group announcement is computed from the same native same-tree radio-button-group algorithm that this component's cross-shadow-root structure breaks (see 2.1.1) — so a set of ct-radio elements sharing a `name` may not be reliably announced as a cohesive group with accurate position/size, even though each individual control's own name/role/value is correct. This is a documented architectural limitation of composing native radio inputs across separate shadow roots, not a per-instance implementer mistake.
ct-radio renders no live-region status messages itself; dynamic validation feedback is ct-field-message's and the implementer's responsibility to expose via aria-live.
